## Discussion

Yak yogurt fermented with traditional starters exhibited distinct profiles in total acidity, characteristic amino acids, and diversity of short-chain fatty acids compared to that fermented with commercial starters. The observed differences are associated with three major areas of metabolic variation supported by the data. First, the variation in total acidity correlates with differing organic acid synthesis pathways. Traditional starters, including L. plantarum, produce both lactic and acetic acids via the phosphoketolase pathway. The interaction between S. thermophilus and L. casei were associated with pyruvate dehydrogenase, leading to butyric acid accumulation and increased total organic acid content (Lang, Wen, Wu, Pan and Wang, 2022a, Lang, Wen, Wu, Pan and Wang, 2022b; Paszczyk & Tońska, 2022). By contrast, commercial starters rely on a single β-galactosidase pathway, causing an imbalance in lactic and acetic acid production and insufficient acidity (Matela et al., 2019). Second, the differences in characteristic amino acids correlate with variations in proteolytic activity. Yak yogurt contains 34% more β-lactoglobulin than regular cow yogurt, offering a unique substrate for traditional starters. The high activity of extracellular peptidases in traditional starters was positively correlated with amino acid accumulation and intracellular pH homeostasis during acidification (Ulmer et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2021). The cell wall proteinase PrtP cleaves κ-casein to release proline, and the intracellular peptidase system (PepX/PepN) breaks down oligopeptides into flavor amino acids such as alanine (Rodríguez-Serrano et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2024a, Yu et al., 2024b). In commercial starters, however, the LacS transporter is overactivated, leading to the synthesis of non-essential amino acids such as glutamic acid, which disrupts the balance between essential and non-essential amino acids (Hashemi et al., 2017). Third, the diversity in short-chain fatty acids correlated with distinct lipid metabolism. In commercial starters, high Lp_3563 lipase activity was positively correlated with long-chain fatty acid enrichment. By contrast, in traditional microbial starters such as L. plantarum A3, the cold-shock protein CspA was upregulated, boosting esterase activity and favoring the synthesis of short-chain fatty acids, such as capric acid (Khademi et al., 2022). This process reduces lipid peroxidation and retains functional lipids such as myristoleic acid. These findings are in alignment with previous findings (Lang et al., 2022).

The profiles of volatile flavor compounds in yak yogurt fermented with traditional starters differ significantly from those in yogurt fermented with commercial starters owing to differences in microbial metabolic synergy. First, regional bacterial communities and raw material characteristics in traditional fermentation were associated with a complex and diverse flavor profile. Commercial starters, designed for uniformity, show a strong positive correlation with ketone synthesis via standardized strains (Yang et al., 2023). Second, bacterial symbiosis and adaptation to challenging conditions are responsible for the flavor complexity associated with traditional fermentation. For instance, in the XZ group, alcohol dehydrogenase was positively correlated with low temperatures to produce ethyl hexanoate; in the QH group, ethyl acetate was associated with the phosphoketolase pathway; in the GN group, Pseudomonas spp. converts linoleic acid into aldehydes in a cold, humid environment. Lactobacillus spp. stabilize aldehydes by synthesizing citrulline through the arginine deiminase pathway, consistent with previous studies (Bintsis & Papademas, 2022; Zhao et al., 2024). Third, the interaction between bacterial metabolic networks were associated with regional flavor profile of yak yogurt. Ketone enrichment in the CK group was strongly correlated with the targeted metabolism of standardized strains (Vénica et al., 2023). By contrast, traditional fermentation groups have varied flavor compositions were correlated with regional diversity. For example, the predominance of alcohols in the XZ group is a result of lactic acid bacteria regenerating coenzymes to form propanol polymers. The abundance of esters in the QH group is a consequence of the interaction between the esterase activity of lactic acid bacteria and short-chain fatty acid substrates. The enrichment of aldehydes and sulfur compounds in the GN group can be attributed to branched-chain amino acid deamination and sulfur metabolism (Liu et al., 2022). In summary, traditional starters were associated with the activate diverse metabolic pathways through microbial synergy and natural selection, whereas the single microbial community in commercial starters was correlated with a more uniform metabolite profile.

Traditional starters exhibit more bacterial diversity than commercial starters. This higher diversity was correlated with regional environmental factors, microbial interactions, and metabolic synergy. First, the traditional fermentation groups in this study (GN, QH, XZ) displayed high Lactobacillus diversity and regional strain enrichment. They create region-specific microbial networks through interactions. By contrast, the CK group maintain microbial uniformity but loses diversity, as demonstrated in previous studies (Huang et al., 2023; Obioha et al., 2021). Second, traditional fermentation groups have more unique species than the CK group, which is a manifestation of the competitive exclusion effect of commercial starters. The high-altitude environment of Tibet favors Firmicutes (96.08%) and L. delbrueckii (49.56%), which enhance cold metabolism through the cspA gene, thus maintaining intracellular pH stability, which is crucial for maintaining high acidity in the XZ group (Peng et al., 2021). The temperature variations in Qinghai was correlated with S. thermophilus, which is efficient in whey proteins to produce esters via β-galactosidase (Li, Yang, Shi, et al., 2024). The grazing environment of Gannan was associated with Pseudomonas spp., which synthesize aldehydes through the lipoxygenase pathway (Zinno et al., 2022). Third, in the XZ and QH groups, Lactobacillus spp. and Streptococcus spp. exhibit a dynamic balance through bacteriocin inhibition and biofilm competition, and this balance is regulated by raw materials rich in fat (promoting membrane lipid synthesis in Lactobacillus spp.) and lactose (promoting glycolysis in Streptococcus spp.) (Brodziak et al., 2021). Commercial starters profiles were characterized by ketone flavor, which is consistent with previous findings (Zhang et al., 2025). Geographically, the XZ and QH groups reflect the convergent evolution of Lactobacillus spp. due to cold plateau environments, while the GN and QH groups reflect the metabolic differences between Pseudomonas and Streptococcus spp. due to rainfall differences (Bai et al., 2024). These associations provide biomarkers for origin tracing, such as the kefir Lactobacillus gene marker in the XZ group (Ding et al., 2022; Peng et al., 2021). Lactobacillus spp. and related bacterial groups drive fermentation. Starter culture type and regional conditions were key factors correlating with final microbial community structure and metabolism.

Interactions among regional characteristics, microbes, and metabolites were correlated with flavor complexity in traditional yak yogurt. Lactic acid bacteria play a key role in this process. L. delbrueckii produces ethyl acetate by converting glucose to pyruvate through glycolysis and glycerolipid metabolism. In acidic conditions, the esterase activity increases, and the esterification efficiency is boosted (Moonga et al., 2021; Shah et al., 2023). Glutamate availability was associated with branched-chain amino acids in Lactobacillus kefiranofaciens, leading to the production of 3-methylbutyl acetate, which confers a fruity aroma (Brodziak et al., 2021). Fatty acids help inhibit the infusion of off-flavors. S. thermophilus suppresses acetone production by blocking fatty acid β-oxidation (ko00071), and this effect can be mitigated by C16:0. L. delbrueckii uses quorum sensing (ko02024) to regulate the ilvE/kivD gene cluster, improving the conversion efficiency of branched-chain amino acids. It also secretes esterases (ko03070) to promote esterification (Rodríguez-Serrano et al., 2018). S. thermophilus maintains energy levels by boosting sugar transport via the phosphotransferase system (ko02060) and oxidative phosphorylation (ko00190). Both strains are synchronized in their metabolic functions through ATP-binding cassette transporters (ko02010), glycolysis (ko00010), fatty acid degradation (ko00071), AMP-associated protein kinase signaling (ko04152), and secretion systems (ko03070) (Zhong et al., 2025).Traditional fermentation groups favor acid-tolerant microbes such as L. delbrueckii, which dominate and shape the community. Amino acids guide bacteria were correlated with specific flavors, and fatty acids control the intensity of flavor inhibition (Matela et al., 2019). Commercial groups, which are lacking in microbial diversity, exhibited a more limited metabolism of flavor compounds (Dan et al., 2019; Uttarwar et al., 2024; Yanting et al., 2025). In summary, the aforementioned pathways contribute to the distinct flavor of yak yogurt from the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau (Li et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2024).

The CK group serves as the gold standard for industrial yak yogurt production. It showed high stability, with highly concentrated clustering of flavor compounds in the principal component analysis plot. Moreover, it displayed microbial uniformity, with a significantly higher Shannon index compared with traditional groups. This ensures controlled fermentation (pH = 4.33, acidity 7.84 g/L) but also reveals three major metabolic deficiencies. From the aspect of nutrition, the presence of Pseudomonadales at a proportion of 25.71% was associated with abnormal accumulation of long-chain fatty acids, with the content of palmitic acid being 8.4-fold higher than that in the GN group. This results in essential amino acid ratios not meeting the standards set by the Food and Agriculture Organization, reflected in the proline content, which was only 35.70% of the proline content in the traditional groups. From the aspect of flavor, a significant negative correlation between C16:0/C18:1n9c content and ester content implies that the activity of esterase is inhibited, resulting in ketones accounting for 62.66% of the total flavor compounds and a severe deficiency of esters. From the functional aspect, microbial diversity does not translate into metabolic advantages because the microbial community is dominated by starch-degrading Lactobacillus and fermenting Lactobacillus. This in sharp contrast with the traditional groups, wherein L. delbrueckii efficiently converts fatty acids into esters after alcohol formation. Overall, the three metabolic deficiencies exposed by commercial starters reveal the core finding of this study—in the unique microecological environment of yak yogurt, the competitive/symbiotic interactions between standardized commercial starters and native yogurt microbiota ultimately lead to indigenous lactic acid bacteria dominating the microbial community structure in the final product. This adaptive deficiency mechanism highlights the ecological niche advantage of traditional starters. On the basis of the advantages of traditional starters in key metabolic mechanisms and quality characteristics, targeted improvements were made to the quality defects in the CK group by transplanting functional strains from traditional fermentation groups. Nutritional improvement was achieved by co-culturing with L. kefir from the XZ group and overexpressing proline iminopeptidase, which activated quorum sensing cross-regulation (ko02024) to increase the proportion of essential amino acids to 65.00%. Flavor optimization involved introducing the L. delbrueckii ester synthase gene (atf1) from the QH group, adding 0.1% sodium butyrate precursor, and incorporating the S. thermophilus phosphotransferase sugar transport system (ko02060). These changes helped increase the ester proportion from 22.03% to 30.00%. Post-acidification control was achieved by integrating the arginine deiminase pathway from ethanol-tolerant Pediococcus of the GN group and combining it with a 0.1% citrate buffer system, which maintained the final storage acidity ≤85°T. In summary, through the technical paradigm of functional module disassembly of traditional strains and targeted enhancement of commercial starters, a dual-stability process of acidity and flavor was developed with stage temperature control and precursor addition, ultimately creating a new paradigm for the CK group that combines traditional flavor with industrial advantages.

## Conclusion

This study highlights the superior physicochemical properties and complex flavor profiles of yak yogurt fermented with traditional starters from the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau compared to commercial starters. Key findings include increased acidity and enriched amino acid and short-chain fatty acid contents, which contribute to unique regional flavors characterized by higher concentrations of esters and alcohols. The functional specialization and coordination of L. delbrueckii and S. thermophilus directs a network of pathways, including glycolysis and ABC transport, to produce defining volatile compounds including 3-methylbutan-1-ol dimer, ethyl acetate, and 2-pentanone. This underscores the importance of interactions between microbial communities and metabolites in flavor formation and provides a rational roadmap for flavor-targeted design in fermented yak yogurt production. Future studies must leverage integrated multi-omics across broader geographical samples to delineate the core microbial and metabolic drivers of yak yogurt quality and the strain-specific pathways linking microbiota to distinct flavor compounds, thereby enabling the rational design of specialized fermentation agents for standardized production.

# Comparative evaluation of yak ghee and crossbred yak ghee: lipid composition, volatile flavour constituents, and microbial community dynamics

**Authors:** Xinyun Yu; Yongqiang Cao; Yiheng Li; Ruiyun Wang; Longlin Wang; Juan Song; Jinliang Zhang; Chengrui Shi; Mailin Song; Weibing Zhang; Fazheng Ren; Pengcheng Wen

**Affiliations:** aCollege of Food Science and Engineering, Gansu Agricultural University, Lanzhou 730070, China | bGansu Chuanqi Dairy Co., Ltd., Lanzhou 730070, China | cDepartment of Nutrition and Health, China Agricultural University, Beijing 100193, China | dGansu Qimu Dairy Co., Ltd., Jiayuguan 735100, China

## Abstract

Yak ghee (YG) and crossbred yak ghee (YD), traditional fermented dairy products central to the diet of pastoralists in China's Tibetan regions, are distinguished by their lipid composition, volatile profiles, and microbial communities. Nevertheless, comprehensive assessments of quality variations in yak ghee sourced from distinct milk origins are scarce. This research systematically contrasted YG and YD concerning their lipid constituents, volatile compounds, and microbial populations to delineate the factors contributing to quality heterogeneity. Lipidomics analysis revealed 43 distinct lipids, with seven glycerides identified as potential biomarkers. A total of 22 volatile compounds were detected, and 3-hydroxy-2-butanone was identified as a characteristic constituent. More than 20 microbial taxa were identified, with Lactobacillus and Lactococcus designated as key differential genera. The observed quality disparities were found to correlate with lipid degradation patterns and microbial metabolism, thereby establishing a foundation for breed identification and quality assurance.

## Abstract

•Comparative lipidomics revealed 43 differential lipids between yak and crossbred yak ghee.•Seven glyceride-dominant lipids serve as potential biomarkers for discrimination.•3-Hydroxy-2-butanone was identified as a key aroma compound in Gannan ghee.•Microbial community shifts were associated with lipid degradation and quality differences.

Comparative lipidomics revealed 43 differential lipids between yak and crossbred yak ghee.

Seven glyceride-dominant lipids serve as potential biomarkers for discrimination.

3-Hydroxy-2-butanone was identified as a key aroma compound in Gannan ghee.

Microbial community shifts were associated with lipid degradation and quality differences.

## Introduction

The yak is a large mammal primarily found in the Tibetan pastoral regions of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau in China. Its unique physiological environment and feeding practices confer a high-quality nutritional profile to yak milk, with notably elevated levels of fat, protein, and minerals, which has earned it the title of “natural concentrated milk” (Fan, Wanapat, Yan, & Hou, 2020; Kalwar et al., 2023). This characteristic also makes it an ideal raw milk source for developing dairy products in the Tibetan region. Ghee, a traditional fermented dairy product derived from yak milk, is produced through preheating, defatting, fermentation, and kneading, yielding a nutrient-rich product (Elbarbary, Jin, & Wang, 2024; Jiang et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2025).

Ghee contains high levels of conjugated linoleic acid, omega-3 fatty acids, and other mono- or polyunsaturated functional lipids, making it a primary dietary nutrient source for herders in the Tibetan region (Kalwar et al., 2023; Li et al., 2011; Mamet et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Moreover, the health benefits of ghee in promoting human well-being have been extensively investigated (Kalwar et al., 2023; Singh, Tyagi, Singh, & Pandey, 2020). For instance, it has been shown to enhance digestion, modulate immune function, and slow ageing processes (Kataria & Singh, 2024; Yang et al., 2024). Therefore, since lipids are the primary constituents of ghee, establishing characteristic lipid profiles and exploring their potential bioactivities are essential for the development of ghee and its derivatives.

Due to their unique genetic background, semi-wild free-grazing system, and seasonal forage availability (Marquardt et al., 2018), yaks show relatively low milk yields (230–400 kg annually, approximately 10% of that of conventional dairy cows). Thus, the increasing market demand for yak dairy products contrasts sharply with the limited volume available for commercialisation. More recently, crossbreeding between yaks and cattle breeds such as Yellow cattle and Jersey has produced hybrids with high-altitude adaptability comparable to purebred yaks. These hybrids exhibit higher milk yields even under low stocking density at lower altitudes (Marquardt et al., 2018) and demonstrate superior milk yield and fatty acid content than purebred yaks (Chen et al., 2025). Moreover, maternal yak milk traits are partially retained yet modified in hybrid offspring. The milk obtained from these hybrids has partially alleviated the supply shortages caused by limited yak milk production (Chen et al., 2025) and has become an important substitute for traditional yak milk in products such as Qula and ghee.

However, ghee quality and flavour are influenced not only by the milk source (Kataria & Singh, 2025) but also by lipid composition and microbial metabolism. Lipidomic analyses have shown that yak milk contains higher levels of unsaturated fatty acids than Simmental milk (Liu et al., 2025). Although Lactococcus, Streptococcus, and Lactobacillus are known to participate in ghee fermentation, they may release extracellular enzymes (e.g., lipases) during storage and transport, accelerating lipid oxidation and hydrolysis and thereby inducing discolouration, nutritional deterioration, and rancid flavours (Liu et al., 2022). The existing studies on this topic have mainly focused on physicochemical (Tian et al., 2023) and oxidative properties (Abid et al., 2017), whereas the combined effects of lipid and microbial diversity on flavour differences between yak ghee and crossbred yak ghee remain unclear.

Lipidomics, a high-throughput analytical approach for comprehensive characterisation of complex lipidomes, has allowed detailed identification of lipid species and structural features (Liu & Rochfort, 2023). It has been widely employed for targeted quantitative analyses of milk fat from different species and lactation stages, including human milk (Zhang et al., 2021), bovine milk (Li et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020), and ghee (Cong et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2025). These studies have demonstrated the reliability of lipidomics in distinguishing ghee derived from various milk sources. Therefore, we hypothesise that integrating gas chromatography (GC)-mass spectrometry (MS), lipidomics, and high-throughput sequencing can elucidate the heterogeneity in ghee from different milk sources and facilitate biomarker identification and quality regulation strategies.

The objectives of this study were as follows: (1) comprehensively identify and quantify the lipid compositions of yak and crossbred yak ghee; (2) compare lipid profiles using multivariate analysis to screen potential lipid biomarkers; (3) characterise key volatile compounds and dominant genera using GC–MS and high-throughput sequencing; and (4) integrate microbial, volatile, and lipidomic data to clarify their interrelationships. These findings will complement existing quality studies and provide insights for process optimisation of traditional ghee.

## Materials and methods

### Ghee sample collection

Yak and crossbred yak ghee samples were collected in July 2024 (summer pasture) from a single herder's grazing site in Luqu County, Gannan Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, Gansu Province, China. To ensure biological representativeness, each type of ghee was derived from pooled milk obtained from the same herd. Milk sampling procedures were in accordance with those described by Guo et al. (2026). After collection, milk samples from each source were pooled separately. The herders then prepared ghee from the collectively collected milk samples under identical environmental conditions. For laboratory analysis, aliquots of the samples were transferred into cryovials, immediately placed in liquid nitrogen for transport to the laboratory, and subsequently stored at −80 °C until further analysis.

The inclusion criteria for all selected animals were as follows: healthy female yaks and crossbred yaks aged 5–6 years with a body weight of 210 ± 20 kg and reared under identical natural grazing conditions without supplemental feeding on the same pasture. All sampled animals were managed under uniform conditions to minimise management-related effects on milk composition.

### Chemicals and reagents

Liquid chromatography (LC)-MS grade isopropyl alcohol and methanol were purchased from Fisher Scientific (Loughborough, UK). Chloroform was obtained from Sinopharm (Shanghai, China). 2-Octanol, sodium chloride, and other reagents were purchased from Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Company.

### Lipidomics analysis

#### Lipid extraction

First, 0.05 g of ghee was added to a centrifuge tube. After adding 750 μL of chloroform-methanol solvent (2:1, v/v), the mixture was vortexed for 30 s, homogenised, and incubated on ice for 40 min. Next, 190 μL of ultrapure water was added, and the mixture was vortexed thoroughly and allowed to phase-separate for 10 min, which was followed by centrifugation at ambient temperature. Subsequently, 300 μL of the organic phase was transferred to a new centrifuge tube, and 500 μL of chloroform-methanol solvent was added to perform a secondary extraction. The organic phases were combined and evaporated under nitrogen or vacuum. The lipid extract was reconstituted in 200 μL of isopropanol and filtered through a 0.22-μm membrane filter to prepare the sample for LC-MS analysis.

#### Lipid analysis

Chromatographic parameters: Gradient elution was conducted on an ACQUITY UPLC® BEH C18 column (1.7 μm, 2.1 × 100 mm) maintained at 50 °C, with an autosampler temperature of 8 °C and a flow rate of 0.25 mL/min. Mobile phase A2 was acetonitrile-water (60:40, supplemented with 0.1% formic acid and 10 mM ammonium formate), while mobile phase B2 was isopropanol-acetonitrile (90:10, containing 0.1% formic acid and 10 mM ammonium formate).

MS analyses were performed using an electrospray ionisation (ESI) source, acquiring data in both positive and negative ion modes. Positive ion spray voltage was set at 3.50 kV, while negative ion spray voltage was set at 2.50 kV. The sheath gas flow was maintained at 30 arb, assist gas at 10 arb, and capillary temperature at 325 °C. The full scan resolution was configured at 35000, covering a mass range of 150–2000 m/z. Secondary fragmentation was performed by higher-energy collisional dissociation (HCD) with a collision energy of 30 eV, and dynamic exclusion was enabled to prevent redundant tandem MS (MS/MS) signals.

#### Data preprocessing

Using LipidSearch (V4.2.28), raw MS data (* .raw) were analysed using the parameters RT tolerance = 0.25 and m-Score threshold = 3 to identify lipid species on the basis of the m/z measurements and their retention time (RT) and peak intensity values. Quantitative normalisation was performed using total ion current normalisation. The annotated lipids in the dataset were classified on the basis of the composition of the fatty acid chain and the modification of the functional groups.

### Volatile organic compound analysis

#### Sample preparation

In accordance with a previously described method (Liang et al., 2025), approximately 6.00 g of ghee was weighed and transferred to a 20-mL headspace vial containing 1.5 g of sodium chloride and 100 μL of 2-octanol internal standard solution (0.001 μg/μL). The vial was sealed with a screw cap. The headspace vial was incubated at 60 °C in a water bath for 30 min. Subsequently, using a manual headspace (HS)-solid-phase microextraction (SPME) device, the extraction fibre was inserted into the vial's headspace, positioning the fibre tip approximately 5 mm above the sample liquid surface. Analyte adsorption was allowed for 30 min. After adsorption, the fibre was promptly inserted into the GC–MS injection port; the analytes were desorbed at 250 °C for 5 min; and chromatographic analysis was performed.

#### GC–MS conditions

GC was performed using the HP-INNOWAX column (60.0 m × 0.25 mm, 0.5 μm) at an injection temperature of 200 °C. The temperature programme was as follows: initial temperature, 60 °C; hold for 1 min; ramp at 2 °C/min to 230 °C; final ramp at 20 °C/min to 245 °C; and hold for 5 min. In the splitless injection mode, the flow rate of the carrier gas (helium) was maintained constant.

The conditions for MS were as follows: ion source and ion monitor temperature, 230 °C and 200 °C, respectively; electron energy, 70 eV; scan mode, full scan; mass range, 50–500 m/z; solvent delay, 3 min.

#### Data preprocessing

In accordance with a previously described methodology (Zhang et al., 2024), qualitative analysis and matching searches for volatile organic compounds (VOCs) were performed using the NIST 11 spectral library, and retention indices (RIs) were calculated. Using 2-octanol as the internal standard, the content of each component in the ghee sample was determined using the internal standard method. The semi-quantitative analysis formula for each component is as follows: m i = m 0 × V 0 × A i V i × A 0

In the equation, mi and m₀ denote the mass concentrations (μg/L and μg/μL) of the unknown substance and internal standard, respectively; Ai and A₀ denote their respective peak areas; while Vi (L) and V₀ (μL) represent the volumes of the ghee sample and internal standard solution used in extraction.

### High-throughput sequencing

Microbial genomic DNA was extracted using the DNeasy PowerSoil Kit (Qiagen, Germany) in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions. DNA concentration and purity were determined using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA), and integrity was verified by 1% agarose gel electrophoresis. DNA samples were diluted to a uniform concentration before amplification.

The V3-V4 hypervariable region of the bacterial 16S rRNA gene was amplified using the universal primers 338F (5′-ACTCCTACGGGAGGCAGCA-3′) and 806R (5′-GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT-3′). PCR amplification was performed in a 25-μL reaction mixture containing 12.5 μL of 2× PCR Master Mix, 1 μL of each primer (10 μM), 2 μL of template DNA, and nuclease-free water to volume. Negative controls without template DNA were included to monitor contamination.

The thermal cycling conditions were as follows: initial denaturation at 98 °C for 5 min; 30 cycles of denaturation at 98 °C for 30 s, annealing at 55 °C for 45 s, and extension at 72 °C for 45 s; and final extension at 72 °C for 5 min and holding at 12 °C. PCR products were verified by 2% agarose gel electrophoresis, and target bands were purified using an Axygen Gel Extraction Kit (Axygen, USA).

Purified amplicons were used to construct sequencing libraries using the Illumina TruSeq DNA kit, and library quality was assessed using an Agilent Bioanalyzer. Libraries were quantified using the QuantiFluor dsDNA system (Promega, USA) and normalised to 2 nM. After pooling, the libraries were denatured with 0.1 mol/L NaOH and sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform (2 × 250-bp paired-end).

### Statistical analysis

The lipidomics analysis included six samples; high-throughput sequencing involved four samples; and GC–MS analysis was performed on three samples. The results are presented as mean ± standard error. Orthogonal partial least-squares discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA), along with community species composition and abundance metrics, were subjected to multivariate statistical analyses utilizing the R package ropls. Subsequently, linear discriminant analysis (LDA) was performed on the BioDeep cloud platform (https://www.biodeep.cn/login) to ascertain differential species influence (LDA score), and a LefSe analysis plot was generated. Screening for differential compounds was conducted based on a p-value <0.05 and a variable importance in projection (VIP) score > 1.0. Lipid biomarkers were identified utilizing the same BioDeep cloud platform. Beta-diversity analysis was performed with QIIME software, followed by calculation of weighted Bray–Curtis similarity to assess differences in community composition among samples. SIMCA 14.1 software was used to perform OPLS-DA analysis of VOCs to calculate VIP values; differential aroma components were screened on the basis of p < 0.05 and VIP ≥ 1. Statistical analyses, including one-way analysis of variance and Duncan's multiple-range test (p < 0.05), were conducted using Origin 2021 (OriginLab, Microsoft Corporation, USA) and SPSS (version 26, USA). Spearman's correlation coefficients were used to analyse correlations among differential lipids, key microorganisms, and characteristic flavours (p < 0.05).

As shown in Fig. 1D, further analysis revealed significant differences (p < 0.05) in the relative levels of BisMePA, CmE, LPC, MGDG, and PE and highly significant differences (p < 0.01) in the relative levels of AcHexCmE, AcHexSiE, CL, LPE, and PC in YG. In this study, the relative levels of PC, PE, and CL in YG were all significantly higher than those in YD. PL undergoes autooxidation due to its structural linkage with unsaturated fatty acids, while PE exhibits a faster oxidation rate than PC due to its higher capacity for chelating pro-oxidant metal ions. Thus, YG may be more susceptible to rancidity than YD.

### Screening of differentially expressed lipids between YG and YD

As shown in Fig. S2, a total of 667 lipids exhibited significant differences between YG and YD. A total of 32 differentially expressed lipid classes were identified across 40 lipid subclasses. Fig. 2E illustrates the significant differences in lipid subclass content between YG and YD. Specifically, BiotinyPE, PG, Cer, PI, dMePE, Hex2Cer, LdMePE, LPE, LPC, and SQDG were enriched in YD, while the levels of CL, SM, PE, DG, AcHexSiE, PC, StE, MGDG, PIP, AcHexCmE, BisMePA, and PS were higher in YG. Yang et al. (2024) also found a higher proportion of PL in yak ghee. These components provide essential lipid nutrition for Tibetan herders in high-altitude regions and help protect against stress-induced damage from the plateau environment (Liu et al., 2022). In comparison with the findings reported by Feng et al. (2025), TG, DG, PE, and PC were common lipids across different milk sources of ghee, while variations in other lipid subclasses may have been influenced by altitude or grazing cycles (Liu et al., 2022). For instance, secondary metabolites in pasture grasses (e.g., polyphenols, terpenoids) have been shown to affect milk fat composition (Cui et al., 2016).

In Fig. 2F, Cer, DG, PC, PE, PS, SM, and TG showed significant interspecies variability between YG and YD, and this variability was primarily distinguished by acyl chain unsaturation levels ranging from zero to ten double bonds, with most variations occurring between zero and five. Notably, the degree of unsaturation is correlated with lipid metabolic regulation: in YD, lipids (DLs) with more than five double bonds were generally downregulated across subclasses, except for Cer and PS, which were upregulated, while DLs with fewer than five double bonds were predominantly upregulated. YD showed an increase in ceramide-upregulated DLs, while DG, TG, PC, and PE exhibited balanced regulation patterns.

These results suggest that PL and NL are key discriminators in lipidomic profiles between the two ghee phenotypes. Additionally, the results highlighted the predominance of medium- and long-chain fatty acids (including both saturated and unsaturated fatty acids), with a small proportion of short-chain fatty acids (C < 6) mainly from the AcHexSiE, DG, and some PC and TG classes. Oxidative degradation of unsaturated fatty acids is the main cause of lipid rancidity (Li et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025). Lipid peroxidation occurs mainly through autooxidation and enzymatic mechanisms facilitated by endogenous and microbial lipases.

### Structural-functional characteristics of differentially expressed lipids between YG and YD

During fermentation, β-oxidation of unsaturated fatty acids generates acetyl-coenzyme A (CoA) for the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, whereas saturated fatty acids undergo β-oxidation to form β-keto acids, which decarboxylate into odd-chain methyl ketones and are subsequently reduced to secondary alcohols by reductases (Feng et al., 2021). The reactive oxygen species generated by lipid oxidation decrease the antioxidant capacity of clarified ghee during storage (Shi et al., 2022). Differential lipid functional enrichment analysis using the LION lipid ontology database identified significant pathways (p < 0.05) from differentially expressed lipid modules detected by Leiden community detection; these pathways are visualised with log10|FDFq| values in Fig. 2G. The top five enriched pathways, namely, plasma membrane, ceramides, sphingomyelin (SP), N-sphingomyelin (ceramide) (SP0201), and lipid signalling, were associated with membrane structure integrity, cellular signalling, and lipid-mediated flavour precursors. This was also observed in the study by Chu et al. (2025). Enrichment was most pronounced for fatty acids with 13 carbon atoms, followed by those with 16–18 carbon atoms, and included polyunsaturated fatty acids, highlighting their potential contributions to ghee flavour development and oxidative stability.

Quantitative analysis revealed that 3-hydroxy-2-butanone was the most abundant aroma-active compound in traditional ghee from Luqu, Gannan. This finding, which has not been previously documented by Feng et al. (2025) or Liang et al. (2025), indicates the potential of 3-hydroxy-2-butanone as a characteristic flavour compound in local ghee. Furthermore, this finding suggests that, beyond processing methods, the milk source significantly contributes to the final aroma, providing a new theoretical perspective on the mechanisms underlying ghee aroma characteristics. Ketones are primarily formed by the oxidation of unsaturated fatty acids, amino acid degradation, or microbial metabolic processes (Zhang et al., 2024; Abdelaziz Elbarbary et al., 2025). Ketones possess distinctive flavours with low thresholds, often displaying a mild fruity aroma (Liang et al., 2025).

Previous studies (Li, Zhang, & Wang, 2012; Yang et al., 2023) have shown that ketones are commonly used as markers to assess oxidative flavours in dairy products, especially milk. For example, the oxidation of linoleic acid predominantly generates 2-heptanone, enhancing the flavour and sweetness of ghee. Aldehydes primarily result from the oxidation of yak milk fat and amino acid conversion, typically contributing pleasant grassy, fatty aromas and fruity flavours (Yang et al., 2023). Alcohols contribute to lipid oxidation and aldehyde reduction. For example, 2,3-butanediol is a key compound produced by lactic acid bacteria during pyruvate catabolism, exhibiting sweet and buttery flavours (Liang et al., 2025). A recent study identified acids as the primary flavour components in Gannan ghee, suggesting that they may serve as substrates for the microbial breakdown of amino acids into esters, thus influencing ghee flavour profiles (Liang et al., 2025). However, this hypothesis requires further validation in future studies.

### Microbial community diversity

In the α-diversity analysis, the Chao1 and richness indices reflect microbial community abundance, while the Shannon and Simpson indices reflect its diversity. Higher values indicate increased bacterial species richness and abundance. As shown in Fig. 4D, the Shannon, Chao1, Simpson, and richness indices for YD were significantly higher than those for YG. Fig. 4E presents the structural similarities in the microbial communities of YG and YD, as calculated using the Bray-Curtis distance. Axis 1 accounts for 98% of the variance, while Axis 2 accounts for 1.4%. YG and YD exhibited distinct microbial distribution separation, and the combined explained variance exceeded 98%, indicating substantial differences in their overall microbial composition. Feng et al. (2025) also found that different milk sources resulted in distinct microbial compositions in clarified ghee.

Species stack plots primarily highlight intergroup differences in species composition. QIIME2 (2019.4) allows for visualization of microbial community distribution across taxonomic levels in the samples. As shown in Figs. 4F and G, YG and YD showed differences in microbial abundance at both the phylum and genus levels. Notably, the microbial communities shared similar compositional categories, but their relative species abundances varied. At the phylum level, the dominant phyla by average relative abundance were Ascomycota (YG: 84.44% vs. YD: 47.59%) and Proteobacteria (YG: 12.85% vs. YD: 4.18%). The findings reported by Feng et al. (2025) suggest that the phylum Basidiomycota dominates microbial diversity in ghee, which is consistent with the results of this study. At the genus level, Lactococcus (YG: 71.32% vs. YD: 42.72%) and Acinetobacter (YG: 7.35% vs. YD: 30.52%) showed relatively high average abundances, although YG had lower overall relative abundances than YD. Studies by Feng et al. (2025) and Liu et al. (2022) both identified Lactobacillus as highly abundant in fresh ghee.

The higher levels of protein, fat, and nutrients in plateau yak milk may promote the growth and metabolic activity of lactic acid bacteria. Lactobacillus, Streptococcus, and Lactococcus—acidogenic microorganisms extensively documented in fermented dairy products—play key roles in the development of flavour profiles (Liu et al., 2024). These bacteria can also reduce the pH of the milk matrix through metabolic activity, thereby inhibiting the growth of harmful microorganisms and contributing to extended shelf life. During fermentation, microorganisms secrete various enzymes to hydrolyse or oxidise lipids, ultimately converting them into small molecules such as aldehydes, alcohols, ketones, and esters, which lead to changes in food flavour (Feng et al., 2021; Wang, Fan, et al., 2023; Wang, Liu, et al., 2023). Chu et al. (2025) indicated that microorganisms facilitate the oxidation and metabolism of lipids such as triglycerides (TG) and phospholipids (PL).

### Linear discriminant analysis effect size

Linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe) was conducted to identify the taxa exhibiting significant compositional differences among groups. As shown in Fig. 4H, genus-level LEfSe analysis identified 20 dominant genera (LDA > 4, p < 0.05), including Lactococcus, Leuconostoc, Streptococcus, Lactobacillus, Roseburia, and Pseudomonas. Among them, Lactococcus, Lactobacillus, and Streptococcus were closely associated with fermentation processes. This observation was consistent with the findings reported by Liu et al. (2022).

However, Feng et al. (2025) reported that Gluconobacter was also dominant in ghee, which could be attributed to differences in milk source and feeding conditions. Furthermore, Feng et al. (2025) demonstrated that Lactococcus and Lactobacillus contribute to the release of VOCs and the production of free fatty acids during ghee processing. Chen, Huang, Yu, and Tian (2020) further showed that Lactobacillus esterases hydrolyse di- and monoglycerides to release short-chain fatty acids and catalyse ester formation from glycerides and alcohols through transferase reactions. Collectively, these findings substantiate the positive contributions of Lactobacillus, Lactococcus, and Streptococcus to ghee quality through lipid metabolism.

PICRUSt predicts functional potential on the basis of characteristic gene sequences. In this study, PICRUSt was integrated with the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database to annotate the functional genes of the bacterial community in ghee. As shown in Fig. 4I, the major enriched pathways included amino acid, carbohydrate, cofactor and vitamin, and lipid metabolism. Lactobacillus, Lactococcus, and Streptococcus may influence the flavour profile of ghee mainly through amino acid and carbohydrate metabolism. Disruption of the bacterial community structure may impair these metabolic functions.

For instance, PE (36:3e) and PE (18:1_22:6) were positively correlated with 2-heptanone (p < 0.05), whereas TG (43:7) and PE (14:1e_18:2) were negatively correlated with n-hexanol, amyl alcohol, and isobutyric acid.

These correlation patterns were consistent with established mechanisms of lipid oxidation. Previous studies have demonstrated that lipid oxidation is a major source of aldehydes and ketones (Chu et al., 2025), and that DG and PE lipids rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids may serve as essential precursors for the formation of key volatile flavour compounds in fish oil (Li, Bai, et al., 2025; Li, Yuan, et al., 2025). In this study, the YG group showed higher unsaturated lipid content than the YD group, which likely accounted for the richer flavour profile of YG, particularly its significantly higher levels of ketones and aldehydes than in YD. Nevertheless, these mechanistic links remained inferential and required experimental validation.

Correlation analysis between key microorganisms and VOCs (Fig. 5B) identified 12 VOCs significantly associated with 14 genera, including Enterobacter_B, Acinetobacter, Chryseobacterium, Enterococcus_B, Gluconobacter_A, Kaistella, Klebsiella, Lactobacillus, Lactococcus_A, Leuconostoc_B, Macrococcus_B, Pseudomonas_E, Rothia, and Streptococcus. Notably, Pseudomonas_E was negatively correlated with most key VOCs. However, Spearman correlation analysis only showed statistical associations and did not support causal inference; therefore, these negative correlations cannot be interpreted as evidence that Pseudomonas_E directly inhibits or reduces volatile formation, even though it is widely recognised as a major spoilage microorganism in milk fat. In contrast, alcohols and ketones were more strongly correlated with Gluconobacter_A, particularly 2-heptanone and 3-hydroxy-2-butanone, whereas acids showed closer associations with Klebsiella and Macrococcus_B.

When integrated with the lipid-VOC network (Fig. 5A), these associations indicate that specific microbial genera and lipid classes co-vary with characteristic volatiles. Genera such as Lactobacillus and Leuconostoc_B were correlated with acids and alcohols, consistent with their known fermentative metabolism. Overall, while specific VOCs were correlated with FFAs and genera such as Bacillus and Lactobacillus, the present network analysis provided associative rather than causal evidence. Future studies combining isotope tracing, targeted lipidomics, and functional assays are required to clarify the mechanistic links among lipid classes, microbial metabolism, and volatile formation in ghee.

## Conclusion

YG and YD showed notable differences in terms of lipid composition, VOCs, and microbial communities. Lipidomics identified 43 differentially expressed lipids, with seven potential lipid biomarkers for each ghee type: DG(16:1_6:0), LPE(22:5), SM(t40:1), TG(18:1_14:0_20:5), TG(20:4e_16:0_18:1), TG(20:4e_18:0_18:1), and TG(4:0_10:0_22:6). Additionally, amplicon sequencing and GC–MS analysis highlighted the roles of Lactococcus, Gluconobacter, and Lactobacillus in ghee aroma production, with 3-hydroxy-2-butanone emerging as a key flavour compound. Correlation analysis suggested that flavour differences may result from lipid oxidation and microbial metabolic activity. These results provide deeper insights into the factors influencing ghee quality. Future studies incorporating flavoromics and metabolomics could track changes over time, facilitate the development of freshness grading models, and improve quality control strategies.

## Exact Asymptotics in the Evaluation of Sequential Experiments and High-Dimensional Models

Abstract

Modern statistical learning procedures and sequential decision-making systems are

increasingly used in settings where reliable performance evaluation and risk assess-

ment are essential. Yet many classical guarantees are organized around conservative

minimax bounds, ﬁxed-target assumptions, or asymptotic regimes that can obscure

the behavior of the adaptive and high-dimensional algorithms used in practice. This

dissertation develops exact asymptotic theory for three related problems: simultane-

ous learning and evaluation in reinforcement learning, risk characterization in high-

dimensional transfer learning, and variable selection under correlated designs.

The ﬁrst part of the dissertation studies oﬀ-policy evaluation in reinforcement learn-

ing. Standard oﬀ-policy evaluation treats the target policy as exogenously ﬁxed,

whereas practical workﬂows often train and evaluate a policy using the same trajec-

tory. This data reuse induces adaptive evaluation bias and can invalidate standard

uncertainty quantiﬁcation. To address this problem, we extend the CRAM method-

ology to Markov Decision Processes, enabling simultaneous learning and evaluation of

a target policy along a single adaptively sampled trajectory without data-ineﬃcient

sample splitting. Under an algorithmic stability condition that controls the discrep-

ancy between consecutive learned policies, we establish consistency and asymptotic

normality of the CRAM estimator and construct a fully data-driven variance estima-

tor. We further verify that this stability condition is compatible with several broad

iii


<!-- Page 6 -->


Thesis advisor: Professor Kosuke Imai Longlin Wang

classes of reinforcement learning algorithms, including policy gradient methods, de-

terministic oﬄine algorithms, and entropy-regularized procedures.

The second part develops exact risk characterizations for high-dimensional transfer

learning under distribution shifts. While multi-stage estimators are commonly used

to combine auxiliary source data with a target environment, their theoretical perfor-

mance has often been described through upper bounds that suppress constants and

procedure-speciﬁc diﬀerences. We introduce Multi-Environment Generalized Long

Approximate Message Passing (GLAMP), an AMP framework that accommodates

matrix-valued iterates, non-separable denoising functions, multiple design matrices,

and anisotropic covariance structures. Through a rigorous state evolution analysis in

the proportional asymptotic regime, we derive exact mean-squared error characteri-

zations for three representative Lasso-based transfer learning methods: the Stacked

Lasso, the Model Averaging Estimator, and the Second-Step Estimator.

The ﬁnal part provides a detailed theoretical comparison of variable selection meth-

ods in sparse linear models with blockwise correlated designs. Moving beyond exact

support recovery, we evaluate performance through the expected Hamming error un-

der a rare-and-weak signal model. We derive exact convergence exponents and cor-

responding phase diagrams for six widely used methods: Lasso, Elastic net, SCAD,

thresholded Lasso, forward selection, and forward backward selection. These phase

transitions delineate regions of Exact Recovery, Almost Full Recovery, and No Re-

covery, and they quantify how correlation structure aﬀects the relative performance

of diﬀerent selection procedures. In particular, the analysis shows how non-convex

penalties such as SCAD mitigate negative-correlation signal cancellation, and how

iv


<!-- Page 7 -->


Thesis advisor: Professor Kosuke Imai Longlin Wang

post-processing and backward elimination can substantially reduce selection error in

the model studied here.

Collectively, this dissertation advances the theoretical evaluation of complex, data-

driven statistical procedures. By moving beyond conservative bounds toward exact

operational limits, it develops mathematically tractable tools for algorithm compari-

son, hyperparameter tuning, and reliable deployment in adaptive and high-dimensional

settings.

## 0 Introduction

Modern statistical learning increasingly concerns procedures whose targets are themselves learned from data. In reinforcement learning, a policy may be trained and evaluated using the same adaptively collected trajectory. In high-dimensional transfer learning, an estimator may combine information from several environments whose distributions diﬀer in both signal and design. In sparse variable selection, the selected model may depend delicately on correlations among a large number of candidate variables. In each case, the object of evaluation is not a ﬁxed, low-dimensional parameter speciﬁed independently of the data, but rather the output of an algorithm operating in a complex stochastic environment. This dissertation studies such problems through the lens of exact asymptotics. Classical theory often provides consistency results, convergence rates, or worst-case guarantees. These results are indispensable, but they may be too coarse to answer many operational questions: How much bias is introduced when the same data are

1


<!-- Page 18 -->


used for learning and evaluation? Which transfer learning estimator has smaller risk under a particular model or design shift? How does correlation change the falsepositive and false-negative tradeoﬀof competing variable selection methods? Answering these questions requires more than upper bounds. It requires sharp limiting descriptions of the actual behavior of the procedures under study. The chapters that follow develop such descriptions in three settings. The technical tools diﬀer across the dissertation: martingale central limit theory and algorithmic stability in Chapter 1, approximate-message-passing state evolution in Chapter 2, and large-deviation phase analysis in Chapter 3. The unifying goal, however, is the same. Each chapter seeks to characterize the performance of a modern statistical procedure precisely enough to support reliable evaluation, meaningful comparison, and principled methodological design. Chapter 1 studies simultaneous learning and evaluation in reinforcement learning. Standard oﬀ-policy evaluation typically assumes that the target policy is ﬁxed while the evaluation data are random [e.g., 91]. In many practical reinforcement learning workﬂows, however, the same data are used both to train a policy and to assess its value. This reuse creates an adaptive evaluation problem: the policy being evaluated is random because it is produced by the learning algorithm, and evaluating it on the same trajectory that produced it can lead to systematically optimistic value estimates. The issue becomes especially important when evaluation is used for model selection or hyperparameter tuning, since maximizing noisy value estimates can amplify this bias. Chapter 1 addresses this problem by extending the CRAM methodology of Jia et al. [83] to Markov Decision Processes. The method evaluates the ﬁnal learned policy by decomposing its value into a telescoping sequence of incremental value changes between consecutive learned policies. Each increment is estimated using later observations from the same trajectory, allowing the procedure to use a single adaptively collected dataset for both learning and evaluation. This avoids the need to reserve a separate hold-out sample, which can be costly in reinforcement learning settings where data collection is sequential and expensive. The main theoretical condition in Chapter 1 is an algorithmic stability requirement

2


<!-- Page 19 -->


for sequential environments. Informally, the learned policies must change smoothly along the trajectory, so that the Jensen-Shannon divergence between neighboring policy iterates decreases at a suitable rate. Under this condition, the CRAM estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal, and the chapter also provides a fully datadriven variance estimator for inference. The stability requirement is then veriﬁed for broad classes of reinforcement learning algorithms, including policy gradient methods, deterministic oﬄine algorithms, and entropy-regularized procedures. Thus, Chapter 1 turns a practical data-reuse problem into a formal inference problem with exact asymptotic guarantees. Chapter 2 turns from sequential decision-making to high-dimensional transfer learning. Transfer learning seeks to improve estimation or prediction in a target environment by borrowing information from related source environments. In highdimensional regression, whether this borrowing helps depends on both model shift and design shift. Existing theory often focuses on minimax rates [10, 105]. Such rates clarify when transfer can be beneﬁcial in principle, but they may hide constants and procedure-speciﬁc behavior that matter when comparing concrete estimators. To obtain sharper comparisons, Chapter 2 introduces Multi-Environment Generalized Long Approximate Message Passing (GLAMP). The framework builds on approximate message passing and generalized AMP ideas from high-dimensional statistics and signal processing [46, 144]. It extends these ideas to a multi-environment setting with multiple design matrices, matrix-valued iterates, non-separable denoising functions, and anisotropic covariance structures. The resulting state evolution gives exact asymptotic characterizations of estimator risk in the proportional asymptotic regime, where the sample sizes and feature dimension grow together. Chapter 2 applies this framework to three representative Lasso-based transfer learning estimators: the Stacked Lasso, the Model Averaging Estimator, and the Second- Step Estimator. These estimators represent diﬀerent ways of combining information across environments: early fusion through pooled estimation, late fusion through averaging separately trained estimators, and target-speciﬁc reﬁnement through a secondstage procedure. For each method, the chapter derives asymptotic mean-squared error formulas under model and design shifts. These formulas provide a procedure-

3


<!-- Page 20 -->


level account of when transfer helps, when it hurts, and how the answer depends on covariance structure, signal heterogeneity, sample allocation, and regularization. Chapter 3 studies sparse variable selection under correlated designs. The Lasso is a canonical method for high-dimensional variable selection, but its ability to recover the true support can be limited by correlations among covariates, as reﬂected in conditions such as the irrepresentable condition [211]. Many alternatives have been proposed, including non-convex penalties such as SCAD [57], ridge-regularized procedures such as the Elastic net [215], post-Lasso thresholding, and iterative forward-backward algorithms. A central question is how these methods compare when exact support recovery is too stringent a criterion. Chapter 3 addresses this question by studying expected Hamming error, the total number of false positives and false negatives. This metric is particularly relevant in high-dimensional scientiﬁc applications, where recovering most signals with relatively few mistakes may be valuable even when exact model recovery is unrealistic. The chapter adopts a rare-and-weak signal model together with a blockwise diagonal design that captures local correlation. Under this model, it derives exact convergence exponents for the Hamming error of six methods: Lasso, Elastic net, SCAD, thresholded Lasso, forward selection, and forward backward selection. These exponents yield phase diagrams that separate regions of Exact Recovery, Almost Full Recovery, and No Recovery. The resulting comparisons show how correlation changes the relative strengths of the methods. In the model studied in Chapter 3, Elastic net acts as a bridge between Lasso and marginal regression and does not improve over Lasso. SCAD improves over Lasso in regimes with negative correlations, where signal cancellation is most severe. Thresholded Lasso improves substantially by separating the control of false positives and false negatives. Forward backward selection often gives the strongest phase diagram among the methods considered. The chapter also connects the blockwise ﬁxed-design analysis to Gaussian random designs, showing that the idealized model captures broader asymptotic phenomena. Taken together, the three chapters advance a common methodological viewpoint: modern statistical procedures should be evaluated not only through worst-case guarantees, but also through precise descriptions of their typical asymptotic behavior in

4


<!-- Page 21 -->


the regimes for which they are designed. Whether the object of interest is the value of a data-dependent policy, the risk of a transfer learning estimator, or the Hamming error of a variable selection method, exact asymptotics provide a sharper language for understanding performance. This dissertation develops that language across three settings where adaptivity, high dimensionality, and dependence make reliable evaluation especially challenging.

## 1 Simultaneous Reinforcement Learning and Oﬀ-policy Evaluation through CRAM

### 1.1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful framework for automating sequential decision making in environments where actions have long-term consequences. It has created substantial real world impacts across a range of application domains, including recommendation systems, resource allocation, robotics, and adaptive interventions. At the same time, the practical deployment of RL systems depends critically on reliable evaluation. Before a learned policy is implemented in a real environment, practitioners typically want quantitative evidence on its expected performance. This need is especially acute in high stakes settings, where errors can be costly or irreversible.

6


<!-- Page 23 -->


For example, in autonomous driving, deploying an inadequately evaluated policy can create immediate safety risks. In healthcare settings such as adaptive mental health interventions or treatment recommendation systems, deploying a poorly evaluated policy may directly aﬀect patient well being. This motivation has led to a large literature on oﬀ-policy evaluation (OPE), which estimates the value of a target policy using data collected under a diﬀerent behavior policy. Most existing OPE methods are designed for settings in which the target policy is treated as ﬁxed while the evaluation data are random [e.g., 104, 181, 186]. Classical approaches include importance sampling and related reweighting methods, which construct unbiased or approximately unbiased estimators by correcting for the mismatch between the behavior and target policies [e.g. 121, 142, 170, 196]. Direct methods instead avoid reweighting by regressing value functions or system dynamics from the oﬄine log [e.g. 73, 100, 207]. Doubly robust methods combine the two approaches to mitigate model misspeciﬁcation while controlling variance [e.g. 51, 85, 91]. However, in many practical RL workﬂows, the policy being evaluated is not exogenously given. Instead, the same dataset is used both to train the policy and to assess its performance. Once the target policy is data dependent, evaluating it on the same data creates a familiar data reuse problem. The resulting adaptive evaluation bias can invalidate the standard uncertainty quantiﬁcation that ignores the policy learning step [52, 134]. The problem becomes even more severe when evaluation is used as part of optimization, for example, to choose among candidate policies or tune hyperparameters. In that case, maximizing noisy oﬀ-policy estimates introduces winner’s curse or maximization bias, leading to systematically optimistic value assessments [165, 173]. A common solution to this problem is sample-splitting, where one part of the data is used to learn the policy or nuisance functions and the remainder is reserved for evaluation [e.g. 40, 134, 136]. Although statistically valid, this remedy can be operationally awkward and data-ineﬃcient in RL settings. In particular, when a single adaptively collected trajectory is available, sample splitting forces the practitioner to decide in advance how much data to allocate to training and when to stop training

7


<!-- Page 24 -->


in order to preserve an evaluation sample. In this paper, we show how to use a single adaptively collected RL dataset to train a policy and to perform a statistically valid evaluation and inference for that same ﬁnal policy. We obtain this simultaneous learning and evaluation of the RL algorithm by extending the CRAM methodology of Jia et al. [83] to reinforcement learning. At a high level, CRAM provides a principled way to evaluate a data dependent target, such as a learned predictor or policy, using the same data that produced it while retaining frequentist statistical validity under suitable regularity conditions. Our setting goes beyond traditional OPE because training and evaluation occur simultaneously along an adaptively sampled Markov Decision Process (MDP) trajectory under a behavior policy. We do not tie the method to a speciﬁc learning algorithm. Instead, we allow practitioners to combine CRAM with a broad class of RL procedures, and we focus on inference for the value of the ﬁnal policy output by the learning algorithm. We establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of CRAM estimator under an appropriate stability condition on the RL algorithm. Informally, this condition requires the discrepancy between two neighboring policies trained along the sample trajectory to become small as the sample size grows. This assumption is closely related to notions of algorithmic stability and regularity that have proven useful for studying generalization and inference in nonsequential i.i.d. settings [e.g. 16, 26]. In our sequential setting, stability provides a tractable route to controlling the additional randomness introduced by reusing the same adaptively generated data both to deﬁne the target policy and to estimate its value. We further show that this requirement is not restrictive by studying the stability properties of common RL algorithms, including policy gradient, ﬁtted Q iteration, and Q learning. To our knowledge, our work is the ﬁrst to provide a reliable evaluation for datadriven target policies trained on the same dataset. Relative to standard OPE, our approach removes the need for a separate evaluation dataset when the goal is inference for the ﬁnal learned policy. We are also the ﬁrst to bring algorithmic stability into sequential learning and to study the stability of common RL algorithms in this context.

### 1.4 The Stability of Common RL Algorithms

The stability condition (Assumption 1.3.2) is a relatively new structural assumption on how policies evolve over time. In this section, we justify its use by discussing three broad classes of algorithms in which policy stabilization occurs: policy gradient algorithms, deterministic algorithms, and entropy-regularized algorithms.

1.4.2 Deterministic Algorithms in Discrete Action Spaces

We next study RL algorithms that generate deterministic policies, namely policies π(·|·) that map each state to a single action rather than to a distribution over actions. That is, π(a|s) = 1 for some a, or simply a = π(s) since the chosen action is unique for a given s. For example, deterministic policies are often obtained by making greedy choices with respect to estimated Q-functions, i.e. π(s) = arg maxa∈A ˆq(s, a) for all s. Deterministic algorithms constitute an important family of oﬄine RL methods. Classical examples include least-squares policy iteration [97] and ﬁtted Q-iteration [56]. 1.4.3 Entropy-Regularized Algorithms

In practice, standard RL objectives and update rules are often augmented with entropy or divergence regularization. Such augmentation can be motivated by the need to maintain adequate exploration or to improve the optimization landscape. These regularizers often heavily penalize point masses, resulting in stochastic rather than

[35], which studies Shannonentropy-regularized natural policy gradient, and Geist et al. [65], which studies regularized MDPs more generally. Notably, Lemma 1 of Cen et al. [35] directly links the increment in the regularized value functions vk−vk−1 to R

Combined with their convergence-rate results (e.g. Theorem 2 therein), this readily translates into a stability condition like Assumption 1.3.2, but at an exponential rate. The second strand regularizes the policy update itself by penalizing or constraining the divergence between consecutive iterates. This approach forms the basis of trustregion methods [151, 152] and policy mirror descent [99, 109, 176, 203]. These algorithms solve a localized optimization problem heavily penalized by a KL/Bregman divergence from the preceding policy. Intuitively, the algorithm must ‘pay’ a KL penalty for every localized change; therefore, a policy update occurs only if the discovered advantage is substantial enough to oﬀset this cost. While these strands are sometimes presented separately, they both inherently force the sequence of policies to stabilize over time through regularization. As the policies approach the optimal action-value manifold during training, the available advantages for value or Q-functions diminish, and the same inequalities that control convergence force the divergence between successive policies to decay toward zero.

### 1.6 Concluding remarks

In this paper, we introduced the CRAM method for oﬀ-policy reinforcement learning (RL), addressing a critical gap in the reliable evaluation of data-dependent target policies. Traditional oﬀ-policy evaluation (OPE) methods typically require the target policy to be exogenously ﬁxed, which forces practitioners to rely on data-ineﬃcient sample splitting to mitigate adaptive evaluation bias when a policy is learned and evaluated on the same dataset. CRAM overcomes this limitation by enabling the simultaneous training and evaluation of an RL policy along a single, adaptively sampled trajectory. By tracking the value of the evolving policy through a telescoping sum of incremental bias corrections, our approach evaluates the ﬁnal learned policy without sacriﬁcing a dedicated hold-out set. A central theoretical contribution of this work is the formalization of an algorithmic stability condition (Assumption 1.3.2) for sequential learning environments. We demonstrated that when the chosen RL algorithm exhibits stability – meaning that the discrepancy between consecutive policies trained along the trajectory diminishes suitably as the sample size grows – the CRAM estimator achieves consistency and asymptotic normality. We showed that this stability requirement is not overly restrictive; it is naturally satisﬁed by a broad class of common RL methodologies, including policy gradient methods, deterministic oﬄine algorithms such as ﬁtted Q-iteration, and entropy-regularized approaches. Building upon such stability, we constructed a fully data-driven variance estimator that facilitates the reliable construction of conﬁ- dence intervals and rigorous hypothesis testing for the ﬁnal policy. The CRAM framework opens several promising directions for future research. First, many of our regularity assumptions leave room for relaxation, such as the overlap assumptions and the assumption that the behavior policy is known, which could be replaced by estimating the behavior policy concurrently with training. Second, CRAM is not limited to the estimation of J(ˆπH); any other estimand that can be cast as an average of inﬂuence functions over transitions can be handled by CRAM, and applications in that regard remain to be explored. Third, an interesting extension would be to study an online, on-policy RL task, where new transitions are

37


<!-- Page 54 -->


generated on the ﬂy by the policies being optimized and are fed to a running CRAM estimator at the same time. The numerical results substantiate the advantages of CRAM over na¨ıve sample splitting. From an application standpoint, evaluating data-driven policies without splitting the sample is particularly vital for high-stakes environments where data collection is expensive. In such cases, CRAM can be particularly helpful. Beyond existing applications in healthcare and autonomous systems, deploying CRAM in complex ﬁnancial modeling and market microstructure settings – where environments are deeply sequential and oﬄine logs are tightly bound to historical execution policies – represents a compelling frontier for empirical validation.

2 Multi-Environment GLAMP: Approximate Message Passing for Transfer Learning with Applications to Lasso-based Estimators

## Abstract

Approximate Message Passing (AMP) algorithms enable precise characterization of certain classes of random objects in the high-dimensional limit, and have found widespread applications in ﬁelds such as signal processing, statistics, and communications. In this work, we introduce Multi-Environment Generalized Long AMP, a novel AMP framework that applies to transfer learning problems with multiple data sources and distribution shifts. We rigorously establish state evolution for multienvironment GLAMP. We demonstrate the utility of this framework by precisely

39


<!-- Page 56 -->


characterizing the risk of three Lasso-based transfer learning estimators for the ﬁrst time: the Stacked Lasso, the Model Averaging Estimator, and the Second Step Estimator. We also demonstrate the remarkable ﬁnite sample accuracy of our theory via extensive simulations.

### 2.1 Introduction

Transfer learning has emerged as a popular paradigm for handling distribution shifts between training and test time. In high-dimensional regression, substantial prior work has derived minimax error bounds demonstrating when auxiliary datasets allow to reduce estimation error and improve convergence rates in transfer learning [10, 29–31, 48, 101, 105, 106, 108, 122, 209]. These error bounds are often conservative, derived for worst-case scenarios, and omit constant factors. Consequently, when applied in practice, the risks for transfer learning based estimators may diﬀer vastly, making it diﬃcult to perform realistic comparisons among estimators. This paper addresses this diﬃculty by introducing a novel approximate message passing framework for tracking the risks of Lasso-inspired estimators in transfer learning. Speciﬁcally, we consider the proportional asymptotics regime, where the number of samples and features both diverge with the ratio converging to a constant. This regime has garnered signiﬁcant attention in high-dimensional statistics and machine learning due to its ability to capture empirical phenomena in moderate to highdimensional/overparametrized problems remarkably well [9, 18, 32, 34, 42, 46, 74, 84, 89, 111, 112, 118, 128, 149, 157, 161, 162, 172, 188, 212]. We introduce a new approximate message passing framework, coined Multi-Environment Generalized Long AMP, that allows to characterize the risk of several transfer learning-based estimators. Concretely, we show the utility of our framework for the following three estimators: the Stacked Lasso [10], the Model Averaging estimator [10], and the Second-Step estimator [105]. To our knowledge, our paper provides the ﬁrst specialized framework for characterizing the precise risks of these transfer learning-based estimators in high dimensions. Approximate message passing (AMP) algorithms were introduced in the com-

40


<!-- Page 57 -->


pressed sensing literature [46] and have seen enormous success in quantifying the risks of convex regularized estimators in high dimensions [13, 44, 63, 132, 161, 162, 188, 201]. In its symmetric formulation, AMP takes as input a random design matrix A ∈RN×N, a sequence of deterministic separable functions ft : RN →RN, and generates a sequence of vectors xt ∈RN in the following way:

xt+1 = Aft(xt) −ft−1(xt−1)B⊤ t ,

where Bt has a speciﬁc form determined by the choice of the denoising functions ft. Remarkably, AMP iterates admit precise characterizations: for each t, as N →∞, xt

behaves as a Gaussian variable with a tractable variance, a property known as state evolution [12, 24]. For a broad range of statistical estimators, one can design suitable AMP iterations that track the estimator of interest (as t additionally diverges to ∞), and thereby obtain exact risk characterization of these estimators. This is particularly useful for studying estimators without closed forms as demonstrated in [13, 44, 161], among others. Since its original introduction, the AMP framework has been extended to Generalized AMP (GAMP) [81, 144], which allows iteration on matrices xt ∈RN×q, and Long AMP (LAMP) [21], which allows ft to be non-separable, and Generalized Long AMP (GLAMP), which allows both [68]. For transfer learning scenarios, the challenge lies in tackling multiple design matrices from diﬀerent environments, as well as anisotropic covariances rising from distribution shifts. To address these, we introduce multi-environment GLAMP, an approximate message passing framework that applies under distribution shift settings. Multi-enrivonment GLAMP tracks iterates from diﬀerent environments simultaneously, while allowing non-separable denoising functions. Remarkably, this combination enables one to track properties of estimators under distribution shifts. We establish rigorous state evolution results for multi-environment GLAMP and show how it can be used to derive precise asymptotic risks for transfer learning estimators. To preview the utility of our framework, we describe our basic setting: we observe E datasets (ye, Xe) with ye ∈Rne, Xe ∈Rne×p from potentially diﬀerent distributions. Each dataset—referred to as an environment—follows a regression model with

41


<!-- Page 58 -->


its own coeﬃcient vector βe (see Assumption 2.4.1). The goal in transfer learning is to leverage information across these environments to improve the estimation of regression coeﬃcients in a speciﬁc environment of interest. Multiple approaches have been proposed for this purpose, and we demonstrate the utility of multi-environment GLAMP by analyzing three representative estimators: (i) Stacked Lasso [10], which serves as an early fusion method by combining all datasets at the start of learning. It solves an empirical risk minimization problem that takes a weighted aggregation of datasets with a usual lasso penalty; (ii) Model Averaging Estimator [10], which represents a late fusion approach by combining information at the end of learning. It computes individual lasso estimators from the environments and then takes their weighted average; (iii) Second-step estimator [105], which follows a pre-training and ﬁne-tuning paradigm. It learns an initial estimator from all but the target environment, and then uses the target data to shrink the ﬁnal estimator toward this initial one. As we will show in Section 2.4, multi-environment GLAMP allows characterizing the mean-squared error (MSE) of these estimators by accounting for both model and distribution shifts across environments. It enables a uniﬁed analysis of these, and potentially a much wider range of transfer learning methods. We further validate our theoretical results through extensive simulations (see Figures 2.4.1, 2.4.2, 2.4.3), demonstrating remarkable accuracy even in ﬁnite samples. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2.2, we provide a more comprehensive overview of related work in AMP and transfer learning. We formally introduce our multi-environment GLAMP formulation in Section 2.3, and demonstrate its applicability for speciﬁc estimators in Section 2.4. Finally, Section 2.5 outlines discussions and future directions.
